\subsection{Transfer-learning protocol}
\label{sec:sota-protocol}

Two pretrained lightweight architectures were adapted to EuroSAT:
MobileNetV2~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}, built from the depthwise separable
blocks of Section~\ref{sec:task2}, and EfficientNet-B0~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}.
Both start from torchvision's ImageNet weights. The final linear layer of each classifier is replaced by a
new ten-class prediction layer, and every run uses the same stratified split,
random seed, augmentation, training-split normalisation statistics, batch
size of 128, 30-epoch budget and Tesla~T4 as the custom models. The checkpoint
is again chosen by lowest validation loss, before the test split is touched.

Once the new prediction layer is in place, there are two options:
keep the pretrained backbone \emph{frozen}, or \emph{fine-tune} it. Each
network was run both ways, so the choice is measured rather than assumed.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Frozen.} Only the new prediction layer is trained, with Adam at
  a learning rate of $10^{-3}$. The backbone acts as a fixed feature extractor,
  and its batch-normalisation statistics are held at their ImageNet values.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuned.} Every weight is trained, starting from the same
  ImageNet weights, with Adam at a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. We chose a rate
  below the frozen-head rate to limit changes to the pretrained filters while
  the new head learns. This is a project choice; the Keras EfficientNet
  fine-tuning example cited by the brief uses $10^{-5}$~\cite{fu2020keras}.
\end{itemize}

The primary runs keep the input at $64\times64$, the resolution the custom
models see. That is the only like-for-like comparison with Model~B, and it is
what an edge device would actually be given. Because ImageNet networks are
designed for $224\times224$ input, a supplementary pair repeats each network
with the $64\times64$ images upsampled to $224\times224$. Each supplementary
pair differs from its primary pair in input size only, so the ablation
isolates what resolution buys.

\label{sec:sota-results}

Table~\ref{tab:sota-comparison} lists both strategies for each network. Two
columns are worth reading together. \emph{Parameters} and \emph{Size} are
identical for the frozen and fine-tuned runs of a network, because freezing
changes what is trained, not what is deployed. \emph{Trained} is where they
differ: a frozen backbone updates only the prediction layer, well under one
per cent of the network, against every weight when fine-tuned. Any accuracy
gap between the two rows of a pair is therefore bought with training effort
alone, at no cost in memory or in operations per image.

For both networks that gap is large. Fine-tuning raises every metric well
above the frozen feature extractor. The likely explanation is a domain shift.
ImageNet filters were learnt on close-range photographs of objects, while
EuroSAT is overhead satellite imagery at a much coarser scale. A frozen
backbone can only re-weight features that were learnt for the wrong kind of
image; fine-tuning lets the filters themselves move towards field boundaries,
road textures and water.

The two architectures also rank differently under the two strategies. Frozen,
EfficientNet-B0 is clearly the weaker network, despite having almost twice
MobileNetV2's parameters. Fine-tuned, the two are practically level. The
frozen gap therefore says how well each network's ImageNet features happen to
transfer to $64\times64$ overhead images, not how much each network can learn.
At $64\times64$, both networks' downsampling stages leave a $2\times2$ final
feature map. Reduced spatial detail may limit frozen-feature transfer, but
this shared reduction alone does not explain EfficientNet-B0's larger
accuracy deficit. Different sensitivity of the pretrained features to input
scale is a possible explanation; these runs do not establish that mechanism.
Once fine-tuned, however, EfficientNet-B0 offers no meaningful accuracy over
MobileNetV2 for nearly twice the memory. MobileNetV2 is the better edge
candidate of the two.

The supplementary rows show that resolution and fine-tuning are partly
substitutes. Upsampling to $224\times224$ gives both frozen backbones a gain of
several points, but the fine-tuned models gain less than one. A frozen
network's filters are fixed at ImageNet's object scale, so enlarging the input
is the only way to bring the data to them. Fine-tuning instead moves the
filters to the data, after which resolution matters much less: for each
network, the fine-tuned $64\times64$ model outperforms the frozen
$224\times224$ one. It does so at about $(224/64)^2\approx12$ times fewer
operations per image, because a convolution's cost scales with the $H\times W$
of its output and the network is otherwise unchanged. For an edge device,
fine-tuning at native resolution is the cheaper way to get accuracy.

Even the smallest of these models is one to two orders of magnitude larger on
disk than Model~B (Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison}). That is why the two tables
use different units. Whether the extra accuracy is worth that memory is the
question Section~\ref{sec:task6} answers.

The training curves (Figures~\ref{fig:sota-loss}--\ref{fig:efficientnet-224-loss})
show the same split between the two strategies for both networks. Each frozen
run levels off at a clearly higher loss than its fine-tuned partner. At
$64\times64$ the frozen runs' training and validation losses stay close
together: the fixed features, not overfitting, limit what the new prediction
layer can learn. The frozen
EfficientNet-B0 curves are also visibly noisier than MobileNetV2's: after the
first few epochs both of its losses fluctuate around a plateau instead of
settling, and at $224\times224$ the lowest validation loss happens to fall early,
so its selected checkpoint comes early in the run. The fine-tuned curves of
both networks are smooth and settle within a few epochs.

The noise in the frozen EfficientNet-B0 curves comes from its fixed features,
not from a training fault. While its validation loss swings from epoch to
epoch, its validation accuracy stays almost level, so the predicted classes
barely change; what moves is the confidence the prediction layer assigns. Two
properties of the frozen features are involved. First, they separate EuroSAT
less well than MobileNetV2's, which is why the frozen EfficientNet-B0 loss sits
higher and its accuracy lower. Second, the two backbones end in different
activations. EfficientNet-B0 uses the unbounded SiLU (Swish)
activation~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}, and a small fraction of images produce
pooled features in the hundreds, where typical values are below one.
MobileNetV2's ReLU6 caps every feature at six~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2},
the bounded behaviour discussed in Section~\ref{sec:activation-choice}. A
small update to the prediction layer then moves the logits of those few images
by a large amount, and with them the loss.

A diagnostic separates the two effects. It retrains only the prediction layer
on the fixed features, with three seeds per setting
(\texttt{scripts/diagnose\_frozen\_head.py}, output in
\texttt{results/frozen\_head\_diagnostic/}). At learning rates of
$3\times10^{-4}$ and $10^{-4}$, EfficientNet-B0 stayed noisier than MobileNetV2
at the same rate, so the frozen-head learning rate is not the cause.
Standardising each feature removes the scale of the large activations. It
roughly halved EfficientNet-B0's fluctuation, to the level of a standardised
MobileNetV2 head, while its loss stayed more than twice as high and its
accuracy several points lower. The unbounded activation range therefore
accounts for most of the extra noise, and the weaker feature separation for
the higher loss. The practical cost lies in checkpoint selection. On a noisy validation curve
the lowest-loss epoch is partly a matter of chance, and it need not be the
run's most accurate epoch. Fine-tuning removes the effect because the backbone
adapts its features to EuroSAT, which is one more reason the comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:task6} uses the fine-tuned runs.

The confusion matrices of the fine-tuned models
(Figures~\ref{fig:mobilenetv2-confusion}--\ref{fig:efficientnet-224-confusion})
place the remaining errors in the same few class pairs for both networks.
Highway and River are confused in both directions; at $64\times64$ both are
thin linear features a few pixels wide. The agricultural and vegetation
classes (AnnualCrop, PermanentCrop, Pasture and HerbaceousVegetation), which
differ mainly in texture, account for a large share of the rest. For EfficientNet-B0,
upsampling to $224\times224$ visibly reduces the Highway--River confusion.
